Hugh Latimer
HYOO LAT-i-mer
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Hugh as English form — actually Germanic Hugo, from hug ("mind, spirit, intellect"), brought into England by the Normans. Surname Latimer from Old French latinier — "a Latinist, an interpreter," originally an occupational name for a clerk skilled in Latin.

See also: Hugh Latimer

📖 Biblical Definition

Hugh Latimer (c. 1487 — October 16, 1555 AD) was the great English Reformer-preacher, sometime Bishop of Worcester (1535-1539, resigned), and one of the three Oxford Martyrs burned by Mary I in 1555-1556. Born to a Leicestershire yeoman-farmer's family; educated at Cambridge (Christ's College and later Clare); ordained priest 1514; held Cambridge fellowships through the 1520s where he gradually moved from energetic Catholic conservatism (he had publicly opposed Erasmus and Luther) to fully Protestant conviction under the influence of his fellow Cambridge man Thomas Bilney. His preaching from the 1530s onward was famous for plain, vigorous, Bible-saturated English, addressed alike to plowmen and to King Edward VI in the royal chapel. Appointed Bishop of Worcester 1535; resigned 1539 rather than affirm Henry VIII's Six Articles which reaffirmed transubstantiation. Imprisoned briefly under Henry, freed at the accession of Edward VI (1547), and through Edward's reign Latimer preached the famous "Plough" and "Lord's Prayer" sermons before the king. At Mary's accession in 1553 he was again arrested, examined at Oxford alongside Cranmer and Ridley, and condemned. On October 16, 1555, he and Nicholas Ridley were burned together at Oxford. As the fires were lit, Latimer (then in his late sixties) turned to Ridley and spoke the words that became among the most famous in English Reformation memory: "Be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man. We shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out."

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

English Reformer-preacher (c. 1487-1555 AD); Bishop of Worcester 1535-1539; preacher to Henry VIII and Edward VI; burned with Nicholas Ridley at Oxford on October 16, 1555 ('We shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out.').

HUGH LATIMER, proper noun. Germanic Hugo ("mind, spirit") + Old French latinier ("a Latinist, an interpreter").

English Reformer-preacher (c. 1487-1555 AD); Bishop of Worcester 1535-1539 (resigned rather than affirm Henry's Six Articles).

Preacher to Henry VIII and Edward VI; famous for plain Bible-saturated English addressed to plowmen and kings alike.

Burned with Nicholas Ridley at Oxford, October 16, 1555: 'Be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man.'

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Latimer is corrupted when his plain-English preaching style is read as anti-intellectual rather than as a deliberate pastoral choice grounded in his Cambridge learning, when the famous Oxford speech is treated as picturesque history without the doctrinal weight it carried, or when his career is reduced to martyrdom without his decades of pulpit fidelity.

expand to see more

Plain-style-as-unlearned misreading. Latimer is celebrated for his vigorous, idiomatic, sometimes salty English (he could call the king's court a 'covetous court' and the priests of his day 'unpreaching prelates' in their hearing). Some modern Catholic and high-church readings cast him as an unlearned populist. The historical record is opposite: he was a Cambridge fellow who had read Erasmus, Luther, and the Greek New Testament; his plain style was a deliberate pastoral choice to address the actual conscience of plowmen and kings alike, not the result of intellectual limitation. The plowman-rhetoric served a Reformed pulpit theology of preaching as God's chosen means of salvation (Rom 10:14).

Candle-speech-as-quaint-history. 'Be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man. We shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out' is sometimes quoted as picturesque Tudor-era memorabilia. The actual setting was an old man burning alive next to his younger friend; the actual claim was theological — that the gospel-light kindled in England by his death and Ridley's would not be extinguished. Mary died in 1558; Elizabeth restored the Reformed Settlement; the candle was not extinguished. The speech was a prophecy that the next half-century vindicated.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Germanic Hugo ("mind, spirit") + Old French latinier ("a Latinist"). The Reformer-preacher Bishop of Worcester (d. 1555); Oxford Martyr.
